1:
Who "the poor" is, and what considering him means, splits the opening four ways. Clarke and Spurgeon take the plain benevolent sense. Clarke makes it imitation — "God is merciful; he will have man to resemble him" — and Spurgeon defines the object broadly: "such as are poor in substance, weak in bodily strength, despised in repute, and desponding in spirit", mostly "avoided and frequently scorned", the world deserting them "as the Amalekite left his dying servant."

Calvin denies the benevolent reading outright. Interpreters generally take the verse of "kindness and compassion manifested in taking care of the miserable", but those who make it "the considerate candour of those who judge wisely and charitably of men in adversity, form a better judgment of his meaning. Indeed, the participle cannot be explained in any other way." The blessing falls not on the almsgiver but on the man who refuses to read affliction as a verdict — David's own grievance, that he "was unjustly blamed by men who regarded him as one who had already been condemned."

Ellicott lays out the options: the Hebrew may be poor, with the ancient versions, or sick, weak in body, or ethically "sick at heart". "The context favours one of the two latter", and the choice turns on whether the sickness is real or figurative; he decides for the physical, since verse 3 "strongly favours" it. He grants the point about the verb without Calvin's conclusion: the word "implies wise as well as kindly consideration."

Gill takes it christologically and singularly. The word is singular, so it "designs our Lord Jesus Christ", elsewhere called poor and needy, "who became poor for our sakes, that we might be enriched by his poverty", and whose "strength was dried up like a potsherd, when he suffered on the cross". Augustine reaches the same reading by his standing rule: Christ "speaketh often of Himself... in His own Person, which is our Head; often in the person of His Body, which are we and His Church; but so that the words sound as from the mouth of one". He preaches it on the Feast of the Martyrs, as belonging to the Passion.

Delitzsch keeps to history and the book's shape: two psalms beginning with ashrey close the First Book, which opened with the same word. He dates it "to the time of the persecution by Absalom", pairs it with Psalm 55, both dwelling "with especial sadness upon some faithless bosom-friend", and rejects the suggestion that the traitor is a type: these psalms carry "the most distinctly impressed individual physiognomy of the writer". Clarke concurs on the occasion and is severe about the messianic reading: our Lord "by accommodation, applies the ninth verse to the treachery of Judas... but as to any other direct reference to Christ, I believe the Psalm has none."

Henry proposes two applications and prefers neither: the blessing may be David's on his friends — "blessed is he that considers poor David", his enemies' provocations having "but endeared his friends so much the more to him" — or David's on himself, who had "the testimony of his conscience... that he had considered the poor" while still at court.

On the promises the voices divide between literal and spiritual. Clarke observes that the benevolent "who search cellars, garrets, back lanes, and such abodes of misery" seldom "fall a prey to their own benevolence", and glosses the turned bed physically: God "hast turned up, tossed, and shaken it... not one lump to prevent him from sleeping.") Ellicott offers the same picture with caution: the Oriental bed was "merely a mat, which could be turned while the sick man was propped up", though "such literalness is not necessary". Gill takes both verses of the soul, the strengthening being "strength in his soul" when "his natural strength and heart fail him". Ellicott corrects "upon the earth" to "in the land".
4:
Ellicott praises the structure: the poet applies the general statement to himself, "and it is a singular mark of the psalmist's sincerity and genuineness that he first looks into his own heart for its evil before exposing that of his friends." Spurgeon hears an argument, "a controversy between the pleader and his God" — the man tender to the poor finds "the promised assistance was not forthcoming" — but notes the restraint: "no appeal is made to justice... he goes straightforward to lay his plea at the feet of mercy." Wesley defines the healing: "the soul is said to be healed, when it is pardoned and purged."

The sickroom visitor is the psalm's most vivid figure, and they differ over who he was. Gill reports "a late learned writer" identifying him with Absalom, visiting his father in the sickness his enemies expected him to die of. Clarke weighs Ahithophel and rejects him — more likely "some other person who was his secret enemy, who pretended to come and inquire after his health, but with the secret design to see whether death was despatching his work". Ellicott insists on a single figure "singled out from the body of enemies", renders vanity as lies, and describes the scene: "pretended sympathy lies at the very bedside, while eye and ear are open to catch up anything that can be retailed abroad or turned into mischief."

Delitzsch links visit to whispering: the intelligence "brought out by hypocritical visitors concerning his critical condition" is what gets spread. Wesley reduces the case to a sentence: "even when he is with me, and pretends hearty affection, his heart is devising mischief against me." Henry catalogues the cruelty: they "had not indeed arrived at that modern pitch of wickedness of poisoning his meat and drink", but insulted him in his sickness, "designing thereby to grieve his spirit, to ruin his reputation, and so to sink his interest". Clarke notes that "it is often a good man's lot to be evil spoken of".

"An evil disease" is the tile's crux, and nobody is sure. Ellicott lays out the ambiguity twice: the noun may be "a lawless speech", "a perverse word", or a physical or moral evil; the verb "may mean 'cleave' or 'pour forth'". Modern scholars prefer the latter, the image from metal-casting, which he judges does not suit the context so well. Gill takes it as no bodily disease but "a word of Belial", a charge of blasphemy and sedition, or else the cross itself, "cursed is he that hangeth on a tree". Clarke splits the difference: "a thing, word, or pestilence of Belial", so that "his disease is of no common sort; it is a diabolical malady", incurable "without a miracle; and he is too much hated of God to have one wrought for him".

The betrayal in verse 9 produces a graded disagreement about the psalm's reach. Gill takes it directly: "the man of my peace... Judas is meant", called and qualified to his office by Christ, and greeted as friend at the betrayal. Clarke leaves the question open — "either a direct prophecy of the treachery of Judas, or... a fact in David's distresses which our Lord found so similar" that he applied it — but presses the Hebrew, "the man of my peace" being the man who kissed him with a greeting of peace "and thus gave the agreed-on signal to my murderers". Wesley states the double sense as doctrine: the words "were literally fulfilled in David, and yet the Holy Ghost looked farther in them, even to Christ and Judas"; the heel he explains from horsemanship, "an unruly horse, which kicks at him that owns and feeds him". Ellicott reports a conjecture that the phrase means "has magnified his fraud against me", and adds that "the rights of Oriental hospitality must be remembered, to bring out all the blackness of the treachery".
10:
"That I may requite them" is the tile's embarrassment, and it is met head on. Spurgeon calls it "a truly Old Testament sentence, and quite aside from the spirit of Christianity", then supplies the defence: David "was a person in magisterial office, and might without any personal revenge, desire to punish those who had insulted his authority and libelled his public character." Wesley gives the same answer in half a line — punishing wicked practices was something "which being now a magistrate, he was obliged to do" — and Spurgeon adds the christological turn, that the great High Priest "had no personal animosities, but even he by his resurrection has requited" his enemies. He also catches the pivot in the verse's first word: "how the hunted and affrighted soul turns to her God! How she seems to take breath with a 'but, thou!'"

Raising up divides between the sickbed and the grave. Clarke keeps it literal — "restore me from this sickness" — allowing that it "has also been applied to our Lord; who, knowing that he must die, prays that he may rise again, and thus disappoint the malice of his enemies". Gill admits no literal sense: it is "not from a bed of illness, nor from a state of poverty and want; but from the dead" — a prayer of faith "founded upon a divine promise", and the resurrection an act of justice as well as power. Spurgeon holds both together: "recover me from my sickness, give me to regain my position. Jesus was raised up from the grave; his descent was ended by an ascent."

The token of favour in verse 11 is read as evidence, not feeling. Clarke argues from the counterfactual: "if thou hadst not been on my side, I had perished by this disease; and then my enemies would have had cause to triumph." Ellicott corrects the tense to a future, "shall know", the restoration being "a sign of the Divine favour, and a pledge of his victory". Wesley grounds it in duration, God having "prolonged my days to the disappointment of their hopes". Spurgeon lowers the bar: "what if the believer has no triumph over his foes, he must be glad that they do not triumph over him."

On the upholding, Ellicott makes the smallest and most telling observation — "here we seem to have the acknowledgment that the prayer just uttered is answered" — where Clarke reads vindication, David standing "under the smiles of thy approbation", applied also "to our Lord... pointing out his mediatorial office at the right hand of God". Wesley renders the last clause "hast confirmed me in thy presence", the office royal and the establishment reaching to David's posterity. Gill takes integrity as sinlessness — freedom from sin "original and actual" — and finds the upholding "especially... by raising him from the dead, when he was openly acquitted."

Everyone recognises the last verse is not part of the psalm. Ellicott says so flatly: "this doxology is no part of the psalm, but a formal close to the first book." Delitzsch adds two details nobody else has: the formula "from aeon to aeon" is, on rabbinic authority, "directed against those who deny the truth of the future world", and the doubled Amen "seals it in a climactic form". Wesley supplies the pattern, each of the Psalter's five books closing so, the doubling showing "the fervency of his spirit". Clarke translates the idiom "from the hidden time to the hidden time; from that which had no beginning to that which has no end", and does what none of the others attempt: collects the ancient renderings — the Chaldee's "and let the righteous say, Amen, and Amen", and the Old Psalter's "Blyssed Lord God of Isrel, fra werld, and in werld". Gill leaves the speaker open: the blessing is the Messiah's or the Church's, breaking out "into an exclamation of praise".
